payload.problem_addressed: Standard test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) derives rewards from answer-level self-voting, which breaks down for code generation because open-vocabulary programs cannot be compared by surface form for majority voting, leaving no usable training signal.
payload.method_summary: Probe-driven TTRL: generate output-free probe inputs from the problem statement, execute candidate programs on them, and score each candidate by a Probe Consensus Reward (PCR) -- the fraction of probes on which its output matches the group's majority output. Entropy-Regularized Rank-Masked Policy Optimization (ERPO) then treats PCR as a conservative negative-only signal: within each candidate group it computes group-normalized GRPO advantages, masks out the top-ranked half (high-PCR candidates), and updates only on the signed advantages of the lower-ranked half, plus a fixed entropy-ceiling regularizer to prevent unbounded entropy drift.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper formulates probe-driven TTRL for code generation, using self-generated, output-free probe inputs to build a behavioral consensus reward (PCR) without oracle tests. It shows PCR is a noisy, asymmetric signal -- more reliable as a negative indicator than a correctness certificate -- and introduces ERPO, a rank-masked, entropy-regularized policy optimization algorithm that exploits this asymmetry. On coding benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests) ERPO improves both pass@1 and the pass@k frontier, including in zero-shot transfer, and pass@1 with a single sample exceeds training-free Best-of-n baselines even at n=32.
key_architecture_choices: Iteratively generated, output-free probe inputs constructed from the problem statement (no oracle outputs required)
Probe Consensus Reward (PCR): fraction of probes where a candidate's execution output falls in the majority output set across the sampled group
Group-normalized GRPO advantage computed from PCR scores, then rank-masked to zero out the top half (high-PCR) candidates per group
Fixed entropy-ceiling regularizer penalizing only entropy above a chosen threshold (Hceil=0.5 used throughout)
payload.headline_results: On LiveCodeBench, ERPO's pass@1 exceeds the training-free Base model's pass@32, and on CodeContests it exceeds Base pass@16; ERPO reaches 36.2% with one sample and no inference-time search, surpassing every Best-of-n configuration tested (CodeT-BoN and RM-BoN selectors stagnate below 30% even at n=32).
claimed_advantages: Builds a usable RL training signal for code generation without any oracle test suite or ground-truth outputs
Improves both pass@1 and the pass@k frontier simultaneously, unlike naive PCR optimization which improves pass@1 at the cost of pass@k
Reduces deployment-time search budget by adapting the model itself rather than relying on more expensive inference-time selection
limitations: Empirical evaluation is limited to competitive-programming-style coding benchmarks; project-level code generation is not evaluated because it requires substantially more engineering infrastructure and compute
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core idea -- constructing a behavioral consensus reward from execution agreement across self-generated probes, then using it only as a conservative negative training signal via rank-masking -- is a plausible template for training hexgen when the frozen verifier's checks are expensive or when supervised imitation data runs out: candidate hex-meshing programs could be grouped, executed by the deterministic mesher, and rank-masked GRPO-style updates could suppress clearly-bad rollouts without over-trusting agreement among candidates as a correctness certificate (directly relevant to care area 6, self-play/verifier-in-the-loop training, and complementary to the existing best-of-N + frozen verifier screening).
payload.reviewer_notes: This targets general code generation (Python-style competitive programming), not CAD/geometric DSLs, so the probe-generation mechanism (LLM invents test inputs from a natural-language problem statement) doesn't transfer directly -- hexgen already has a much stronger, deterministic verifier (compiles, zero inverted elements, quality bounds) rather than a noisy self-consistency proxy, so PCR's core motivation (no oracle available) is less pressing here. The transferable piece is narrower: the rank-masking/entropy-ceiling recipe as a stable way to do RL against a partially-trusted signal, useful if the pipeline ever adds a softer reward on top of the frozen verifier.

payload.problem_addressed: In repository-level code repair, the official evaluator is hidden, so an agent must construct and trust its own validation tests; when the same trajectory writes both the patch and the test, their errors can agree and create false confidence that a wrong patch is correct.
payload.method_summary: A test-verify-revise scaffold separates test construction from source repair: a Test agent independently generates a repository-native regression test bundle (test patch + execution command + behavior contract), a fail-closed harness qualifies/freezes it (requiring a clean failure on the buggy repo), and a Repair agent then revises source code from the fixed test's execution feedback without being able to alter the test. Both Test and Repair agents (Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B) are trained separately with role-specific RL: the Test agent is rewarded for producing behaviorally valid, discriminative tests; the Repair agent is rewarded for direct resolution and feedback-conditioned revision.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces ExecCritic, a scaffold that keeps test generation and source repair as separate roles/agents so the validation evidence used to stop repair cannot be gamed by the same trajectory that wrote the patch. It trains a Test agent to produce reliable, discriminative repository-native tests and a Repair agent to revise source code from that fixed feedback via role-specific RL. On SWE-bench Verified, the composed trained system reaches 72.6% resolved, an 11.4-point gain over a no-test baseline, without using a stronger model or oracle feedback at evaluation time.
key_architecture_choices: Two separate agents/policies: a Test agent and a Repair agent, both built on Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B, trained with different RL objectives
Fail-closed harness that qualifies a Test bundle by requiring it to execute and fail cleanly on the buggy (Base) repository before being frozen
Test bundle = repository-native test patch + exact execution command + structured JSON behavior contract
Repair agent revises only the source patch across rounds using bounded execution feedback from the frozen test
payload.headline_results: Holding the base Repair agent fixed, tests from the base Test agent reduce resolved rate from a no-test baseline of 61.2% to 57.3%, whereas tests from GPT-5.6-sol raise it to 65.3%; role-specific post-training raises the Qwen Test agent's Base-to-Gold success from 22.2% to 62.2%, and composing the two post-trained Qwen agents reaches 72.6%, an 11.4-point gain over the original no-test baseline.
claimed_advantages: Prevents the Repair agent from weakening its own validation criteria to accommodate a candidate patch, since the test is generated independently and frozen
Isolates and separately improves two distinct capabilities (test construction vs. repair) rather than relying on general coding ability to do both
Achieves gains without a stronger model or oracle feedback at evaluation time
limitations: Test and Repair are trained as separate policies rather than a single shared-weight model with role conditioning, which would simplify deployment and allow end-to-end optimization
Generated-test feedback can help or harm repair depending on test quality: weak self-generated tests actively reduced resolved rate relative to no test at all
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The core structural idea -- keeping the artifact that judges correctness independent of and frozen relative to the artifact being generated/repaired -- maps directly onto hexgen's structural-validity problem: it suggests that a self-critiquing or self-testing loop for hex-mesh programs should not let the same model rollout that produced a candidate program also decide when to stop revising it, reinforcing the value of hexgen's already-frozen, machine-checkable verifier as the independent judge. The 'Learn to Test' role-specific RL recipe (rewarding valid, discriminative checks; separately rewarding feedback-conditioned revision) is a template for training a repair/edit-distillation policy (care area 1: DAgger-style learning to fix a model's own broken rollouts) that revises a hexgen program using structured feedback from the frozen verifier.
payload.reviewer_notes: Domain is software repository repair (SWE-bench), not CAD/geometry, so nothing here transfers on data or architecture -- the transferable content is purely the training-loop design pattern (independent, frozen verification signal + specialized repair policy trained against it). Authors note the two-policy design adds engineering overhead versus a single shared-weight model; a hexgen adaptation would need to substitute the frozen mesh verifier for the learned Test agent, which is arguably simpler since hexgen's verifier is already deterministic and machine-checkable rather than learned.

payload.problem_addressed: MCTS-based self-play (e.g. AlphaZero) is the dominant paradigm for game-playing agents but carries substantial computational overhead from search during both training and inference; it is unclear how much of this cost is necessary versus how well a much simpler direct value-learning approach could do.
payload.method_summary: A minimal self-play implementation of Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) using only epsilon-greedy self-play, one-step negamax backups, and a neural value function -- no tree search during training. Evaluated with ground-truth oracles on Connect Four, Hex(7x7), and synthetic F-Games (exact value error and policy regret measurable), and with a MiniZero AlphaZero baseline on the larger Othello and Go(9x9).
payload.contributions_summary: The paper provides the first systematic oracle-based comparison of neural AVI and MCTS-based self-play (AlphaZero) across multiple non-trivial games, measuring value error, policy regret, and play against perfect oracles. It shows AVI learns substantially more accurate value functions than an AlphaZero baseline, that its one-step-lookahead greedy policies remain competitive with MCTS-based policies at much lower training/inference cost, and that AVI trains stably on larger games (Othello, Go 9x9), with learned values that improve MiniZero's playing strength when substituted into the same MCTS inference budget.
key_architecture_choices: Epsilon-greedy self-play with one-step negamax value backups (no tree search during training)
Neural value function trained via direct value learning (bootstrapping + function approximation + off-policy data, i.e. the RL 'deadly triad' combination)
Cross-inference experiments: plugging AVI-learned values into an MCTS inference procedure (e.g. MiniZero) instead of only greedy one-step lookahead
payload.headline_results: AVI learns substantially more accurate value functions than the AlphaZero baseline while its one-step-lookahead greedy policies remain competitive with MCTS-based policies at substantially lower training and inference cost; on Othello and Go(9x9), AVI-learned values improve MiniZero's playing strength when used with the same MCTS inference budget.
claimed_advantages: Trains stably across domains and random seeds despite combining function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy learning (the 'deadly triad')
Learns more accurate value functions than AlphaZero at far lower training and inference cost (no tree search needed during training)
Learned values remain useful as a drop-in improvement for MCTS-based inference on larger games, showing training and inference can be designed separately
limitations: Strongest claims rest on exact oracle evaluation and therefore concern only Connect Four, Hex(7x7), and F-Games; Othello and Go(9x9) results are benchmarked only against a fixed MiniZero baseline and cannot reveal true distance from optimal play
Games at the scale of Go(19x19) or Chess were not tested
The forward-equivalent compute proxy captures the main neural-network cost but not every source of wall-clock overhead (e.g. building/populating MCTS trees)
On Othello and Go(9x9), greedy AVI spreads its exploration budget evenly across every legal action rather than toward promising moves
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: hexgen's frozen verifier plus best-of-N screening is itself a form of self-play/verifier-in-the-loop training (care area 6); this paper suggests that a much simpler direct value-learning signal (a learned critic trained by one-step negamax-style backups over partial hex-meshing program prefixes, scored against verifier outcomes) could substitute for or complement full MCTS/beam search over program prefixes (care area 1) at substantially lower training and inference cost, while still improving decision quality if later combined with search at deployment time (the cross-inference finding). The finding that error propagation may behave better in alternating/adversarial value backups is a useful prior if hexgen ever frames program construction as an adversarial or verifier-vs-generator game.
payload.reviewer_notes: Domain is board games with much larger action/state spaces explored via self-play against a fixed opponent (or itself), not autoregressive program generation against a static verifier -- the negamax/alternating-player framing doesn't map cleanly onto single-agent program synthesis, so the transfer is at the level of 'simple value learning can rival search-heavy methods' rather than a directly reusable algorithm. Authors themselves caution the stability result is empirical, not proven, and may be specific to the alternating-game structure.

provenance.problem_addressed: the computational overhead of the most popular methods, based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), can be substantial
provenance.method_summary: We train a minimal self-play implementation of Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) and use ground-truth oracles for exact evaluation.
provenance.contributions_summary: We show that AVI learns substantially more accurate value functions than our AlphaZero baseline. Its one-step-lookahead policies remain competitive at substantially lower cost
provenance.headline_results: AVI learns substantially more accurate value functions than our AlphaZero baseline, and does so stably across random seeds
provenance.claimed_advantages: the expected failure mode does not materialize in our experiments: AVI trains stably across domains and random seeds while learning increasingly accurate value functions
provenance.limitations: the Othello and Go(9x9) experiments, by contrast, are benchmarked only against a fixed MiniZero baseline and cannot reveal how far either agent is from optimal play

payload.problem_addressed: In GRPO-style RLVR, prompt groups where all rollouts are correct or all wrong ('silent groups') have identically zero group-relative advantage and contribute no reward-advantage gradient, yet uniform sampling wastes a large fraction of rollouts on them; history-based selectors that could avoid this must first spend rollouts to estimate a prompt's difficulty, creating a cold start.
payload.method_summary: ThinkPrior is a zero-rollout difficulty prior: before training starts, a small off-the-shelf 'anchor' model is run once, offline, over the prompt pool and scored by the same verifier used in training; its pass rate initializes a Beta posterior over each prompt's difficulty/learnability. Training then selects prompts by expected learnability from this posterior (no target-policy rollouts needed for the first selection) and updates the posterior from real target-policy outcomes as training proceeds, without changing the loss or optimizer.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper identifies and quantifies the cost of 'silent groups' in GRPO-based RLVR (up to 39% of rollouts contribute no gradient) and shows the problem is worse early in training because per-prompt difficulty is unknown ('cold start'). It introduces ThinkPrior, a zero-rollout difficulty prior built from an external, offline anchor pass, and shows on Qwen2.5-Math-7B across sixteen seeds that it more than halves early silent groups and cuts wasted rollouts through step 30 by nearly a fifth, while final accuracy is unchanged; a ThinkPrior+DAPO composition reduces total generated rollouts by 10.6% at matched update budget.
key_architecture_choices: External-anchor initialization for a per-prompt Beta posterior over 'learnability', computed from a cheap offline model's verifier-scored pass rate on the prompt pool before any target-policy rollout
Prompt selection by expected posterior learnability rather than by observed target-policy history
Posterior updated online from real training outcomes after the cold-start phase, layering onto existing selection mechanisms without changing loss or optimizer
payload.headline_results: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B across sixteen seeds, ThinkPrior more than halves early silent groups (from 23.8% to 10.6%, a 55% relative reduction) and cuts wasted rollouts through step 30 by 19%, with no detected difference in final accuracy; the measured ThinkPrior+DAPO composition reduces generated rollouts by 10.6% at the same 3840-rollout update budget.
claimed_advantages: Requires no target-policy rollout before the very first prompt selection, unlike history-based difficulty estimators
Changes neither the training loss nor the optimizer -- a drop-in prompt-selection prior
Reduces early wasted compute (silent-group generation and verification cost) without hurting final accuracy
limitations: On the primary 250-prompt pool, the fixed-budget result is a reallocation of compute rather than a net saving; only the ThinkPrior+DAPO composition shows a measured net generation reduction
Evidence supports a cold-start benefit from the prior but does not establish pool exhaustion, component-level causality, or a general stability effect
Code, complete data, and training trajectories are not currently public
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: hexgen's training data (inverse-factory-sampled and auto-labeled real-CAD programs) likely has a wide range of per-example difficulty; if hexgen is ever trained with RLVR-style updates against the frozen verifier's pass/fail signal (a natural extension of care area 6, self-play/verifier-in-the-loop training), ThinkPrior's zero-rollout, offline difficulty prior -- scored by a cheap proxy model or heuristic and used to avoid spending best-of-N verifier calls on B-reps whose programs are already trivially easy or all-fail -- is a directly transferable curriculum/data-selection mechanism to reduce wasted verifier calls during training, especially in the cold-start phase before the model has any track record on a given B-rep.
payload.reviewer_notes: Domain and reward structure (math RLVR with GRPO, verifiable scalar reward) are structurally close to how hexgen could train against its frozen verifier, making this one of the more directly transferable papers in this batch despite the different application area. The headline result is explicitly a compute-reallocation, not an accuracy improvement, so the practical payoff for hexgen would be training-efficiency rather than backlog quality per se.

provenance.method_summary: a small off-the-shelf anchor runs the pool offline, scored by the same verifier used in training, and its pass rate supplies an external-anchor initialization for a Beta posterior
provenance.contributions_summary: ThinkPrior more than halves early silent groups and cuts wasted rollouts through step 3030 by nearly a fifth, while we detect no difference in final accuracy
provenance.headline_results: more than halves silent groups in early training—from 23.8%23.8\% to 10.6%10.6\% over sixteen seeds, a 55%55\% relative reduction

payload.problem_addressed: Classical Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (CVT) solvers for high-quality surface remeshing/sampling are computationally expensive because each optimization step must reconstruct restricted Voronoi diagrams and re-integrate per-cell quantities, limiting CVT to offline preprocessing rather than interactive or learning-in-the-loop pipelines.
payload.method_summary: Neural CVT replaces classical iterative CVT solvers with a learned recurrent optimizer. A graph neural encoder extracts multi-scale geometric descriptors from a dense point cloud sampled from the input surface; a lightweight recurrent (GRU-based) optimizer then refines seed positions over a small, fixed number of iterations, aggregating interpolated surface features and optimization history to predict per-seed displacements. The whole system is trained end-to-end and self-supervised using the explicit CVT energy (isotropic and, optionally, feature-aligned loss terms) as the training signal -- no ground-truth seed positions are needed.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces Neural CVT, a learning-based surface-CVT solver that couples a geometric feature extractor with a recurrent neural optimizer to predict seed displacements over a small number of steps, trained self-supervised on the CVT energy itself. It demonstrates generalization to unseen organic and CAD-like shapes, initialization strategies, and seed densities, producing isotropic, feature-preserving remeshes comparable to state-of-the-art offline optimizers while accelerating CVT optimization by one to two orders of magnitude.
key_architecture_choices: Graph neural geometry encoder computing multi-scale descriptors (curvature, part boundaries, target density) on a dense point cloud sampled from the input surface

Recurrent (GRU-based) optimizer with a seed encoder and seed decoder that predicts per-seed displacements over a small, fixed number of iterations, using interpolated surface features plus optimization history
Self-supervised training directly on the classical CVT energy (isotropic CVT loss, plus a feature-aligned loss variant for sharp-feature preservation)
Restricted Voronoi Diagram (RVD)-based final mesh extraction from the optimized seed positions
datasets: diverse organic and CAD-like 3D shape collection (up to 50K input / 3K output points)
payload.headline_results: Neural CVT accelerates CVT optimization by one to two orders of magnitude compared with traditional geometric optimization while producing isotropic, feature-preserving remeshes comparable in quality to state-of-the-art offline methods, and generalizes to unseen shapes, initializations, and seed densities.
claimed_advantages: One to two orders of magnitude faster than classical Lloyd's-method/L-BFGS CVT solvers by amortizing the geometric feature extraction and avoiding repeated Voronoi-diagram reconstruction
Generalizes to unseen geometry, initialization strategies, and seed densities without retraining
Handles both smooth organic shapes and CAD-like models with sharp edges/corners
limitations: RVD-based mesh extraction struggles with thin/slender structures at low resolutions, producing topological errors (holes, non-manifold artifacts) that only improve with higher seed counts
Input/output sizes are capped (50K input points, 3K output points) due to GPU memory and training time; scaling beyond this degrades remeshing quality

As a data-driven method, it lacks theoretical guarantees of convergence to the global minimum, and is best used as a fast initialization for a traditional solver rather than a final-answer replacement
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: hexgen's mesher executes generated programs to produce all-hexahedral meshes and its verifier checks scaled-Jacobian/aspect-ratio quality and strict parametric surface-match boundary fidelity -- Neural CVT's core mechanism (a graph/point-cloud encoder + a small-step recurrent optimizer trained self-supervised directly on a classical geometric energy, replacing an expensive combinatorial reconstruction with a few learned steps) is a directly transferable pattern for building a fast learned proxy or initializer for parts of the hex-meshing pipeline (e.g., seed/vertex placement, quality-driven local geometry repair) rather than for the program-generation decoder itself; its demonstrated success on CAD-like models with sharp features (Figure 1) is a relevant existence proof that neural methods generalize to CAD geometry with hard mechanical-part features similar to hexgen's B-rep inputs.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a computer-graphics remeshing paper (triangle surface meshes and CVT), not a hex-meshing DSL/program-generation paper, so it does not bear on structural-validity-of-generated-programs or B-rep-to-program decoding directly; the value is as a design pattern for learned geometric solvers and as evidence that learned methods trained self-supervised on a classical quality energy can match offline optimizers on CAD-like inputs.

provenance.problem_addressed: computing surface CVTs with classical solvers remains expensive: each optimization step repeatedly constructs restricted Voronoi diagrams (RVDs) and integrates quantities over their surface cells
provenance.method_summary: A lightweight recurrent optimizer then refines seed positions over a small number of iterations, aggregating interpolated surface features and optimization history to predict per-seed displacements.
provenance.contributions_summary: accelerating CVT optimization by one to two orders of magnitude in our benchmarks while preserving geometric fidelity
provenance.headline_results: our solver accelerates iterative optimization by one to two orders of magnitude compared with traditional geometric optimization

payload.problem_addressed: Equivariant networks are commonly trained with Adam, but matrix-structured optimizers such as Muon empirically perform better on them without an explained mechanism; the paper identifies why -- Adam applies one global learning rate that produces unequal spectral step sizes across the different irrep blocks of an equivariant linear layer.
payload.method_summary: Each irrep block of degree l in an equivariant linear layer shares a channel-mixing matrix W_l across its 2l+1 components, so its gradient has rank at most 2l+1 and Adam's per-weight rescaling (which ignores irrep-block boundaries) produces different spectral step sizes per block under one global learning rate. The paper introduces a parameter-free block-normalization rule that rescales each block's update to a fixed spectral step (matching what Muon does via SVD polar decomposition) without changing Adam's moment estimates or update direction within a block, and separately evaluates tuning Adam's momentum coefficients.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper identifies and characterizes an intra-layer learning-rate mismatch specific to equivariant networks: different irrep blocks receive different spectral step sizes under a single global Adam learning rate because of their differing gradient-rank structure. It introduces a parameter-free blockwise normalization rule that removes this mismatch, and shows in a controlled SO(3)-equivariant model and an e3nn interatomic potential model (trained on rMD17 and MD22) that combining block normalization with tuned Adam momentum coefficients makes Adam competitive with or better than Muon, explaining much of Muon's previously unexplained advantage on equivariant architectures.
key_architecture_choices: Parameter-free blockwise normalization: rescale each irrep block's Adam update to spectral step size eta, leaving Adam's moment estimates and within-block update direction unchanged
Separately tuned Adam moment coefficients (beta1, beta2), selected after normalization
Controlled SO(3)-equivariant toy model with matched dense (non-equivariant) MLP control, plus a NequIP-style e3nn interatomic potential model with gated tensor-product interaction layers
metrics: spectral step size ratio across blocks

payload.problem_addressed: Embodied planning increasingly relies on vision-language models (VLMs) to produce executable action sequences, but fluent plans are not always executable: a VLM may reference objects not visually observed, select actions with unavailable affordances, or violate syntax/action constraints.
payload.method_summary: CLAMP is a multimodal constraint-grounding framework: it uses the initial scene observation to restrict object references to visually-supported entities, while a provided symbolic action model specifies state transitions and goals. During decoding, hard masks eliminate invalid next-token candidates, and a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based world-state lookahead module reweights the remaining feasible candidates' probabilities based on action preconditions and goal reachability -- keeping the frozen VLM's language prior while filtering out unsupported, unsafe, or infeasible plan steps. For unseen tasks/environments, the HMM is adapted at test time using label-free continuations sampled from the frozen VLM.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper introduces CLAMP, a decoding-time constrained-generation framework for embodied planning with frozen VLMs that combines hard token masking (from scene-grounded object references and a symbolic action model) with an HMM-based lookahead that reweights candidates by precondition and goal-reachability feasibility. It shows on VLABench, SafeAgentBench, and TaPA that these scene-grounded constraints improve object grounding and safety in generated plans, with most remaining failures attributed to perception errors or misaligned constraint specifications.
key_architecture_choices: Frozen VLM planner with decoding-time hard token masks derived from scene observation and a symbolic action model
HMM-based world-state lookahead module that reweights feasible candidate tokens by action preconditions and goal reachability
Test-time HMM adaptation for unseen tasks/environments using label-free continuations sampled from the frozen VLM
payload.headline_results: Scene-grounded constraints improve object grounding and safety on VLABench, SafeAgentBench, and TaPA, while most remaining failures stem from perception errors or misaligned constraint specifications.
claimed_advantages: Retains the frozen VLM's language prior while preventing visually unsupported, unsafe, or infeasible candidates from entering the plan
Adapts to unseen tasks and environments via label-free test-time HMM adaptation, without retraining the VLM
limitations: Most remaining failures stem from perception errors or misaligned constraint specifications
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: The decoding-time hard-mask + HMM-based feasibility-reweighting mechanism is directly transferable to hexgen's core structural-validity problem (care area 1): masking out program tokens that would reference faces not present in the input B-rep or violate a hex-meshing command's preconditions, and reweighting remaining candidates by a lookahead estimate of whether the partial program can still reach a state that will pass the frozen verifier (analogous to CLAMP's 'goal reachability'). The test-time, label-free adaptation of the feasibility model to unseen environments is also a plausible mechanism for domain-gap mitigation (care area 2) between the synthetic 'inverse factory' training distribution and real, auto-labeled CAD parts.
